paragraphs: The paper studies how to maximize an unknown function while observing its value as few times as possible. The search takes place over a compact, convex set. Its central idea is that optimization depends heavily on learning which inputs are better than others, making ranking a useful route to finding good solutions.

The authors connect global optimization to bipartite ranking and introduce general optimization procedures that can use a chosen ranking method. This connection provides a way to address high-dimensional inputs and functions with weak regularity properties. The approach organizes the search around the function’s ordering structure, giving ranking methods a direct role in deciding where to search.

The paper supplies theoretical properties and convergence guarantees, and also derives equivalences between several optimization methods. Its main algorithm adapts empirically to the underlying ranking structure. Numerical results on typical benchmarks indicate that it generally outperforms the existing global optimization algorithms considered, supporting the practical value of the ranking perspective.
icml-2016-a-ranking-approach-to-global-o.tldr: The paper turns global optimization into a ranking problem to guide an observation-efficient search for high-value inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic multi-armed bandits, where a learner repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards. The challenge is to learn about the options while making useful choices along the way. The authors introduce an anytime algorithm, meaning its operation does not require a fixed stopping time to be specified in advance.

The main theoretical contribution is optimal bounds of two kinds, for a specific family of parameters. Distribution-free bounds describe performance without tailoring the guarantee to a particular reward distribution. Distribution-dependent bounds capture how performance varies with the underlying problem. Having both types of results provides complementary ways to assess the algorithm, while the parameter qualification defines the scope of the optimality claim.

The authors empirically evaluate this algorithm and another motivated by a conjectured optimal bound. They also give a similar analysis in the full-information setting as a benchmark. This comparison separates the bandit setting’s limited feedback from a setting with more information, providing context for interpreting the proposed methods.
icml-2016-anytime-optimal-algorithms-in-.tldr: An anytime stochastic bandit algorithm achieves optimal distribution-free and distribution-dependent bounds for a specified parameter family.

paragraphs: An autoencoder needs a way to judge how closely a reconstruction resembles its input. This paper replaces element-by-element comparison with a comparison based on learned features. The aim is to measure similarity in a way that better reflects the data’s structure and can offer invariance to changes such as translation.

The method combines a variational autoencoder with a generative adversarial network. Representations learned by the adversarial network’s discriminator become the basis of the autoencoder’s reconstruction objective. Reconstruction errors are therefore measured in feature space. The discriminator supplies a learned description of the images, which the autoencoder uses to assess the quality of its reconstructions.

On face images, the authors report better visual fidelity than variational autoencoders using element-wise similarity measures. They also show that the learned embedding supports simple arithmetic changes to high-level visual properties, including whether a face wears glasses. These results connect the choice of reconstruction objective to both image appearance and the usefulness of the learned representation for visual editing.
icml-2016-autoencoding-beyond-pixels-usi.tldr: Combining a VAE with GAN discriminator features improves face-image fidelity and enables simple edits to abstract visual attributes.

paragraphs: Deep generative models use neural networks to represent how data may be generated, but learning also depends on how well their hidden uncertainty can be approximated. This paper improves that approximation by adding auxiliary variables. These variables make the variational distribution more expressive while leaving the underlying generative model unchanged.

That distinction is central to the contribution: a richer approximation can improve learning without requiring the original data-generating model to change. The authors also use the structure of the auxiliary variable to motivate a separate model with two stochastic layers and skip connections. The paper therefore explores both a more flexible inference construction and an architecture inspired by it.

The findings suggest that expressive, appropriately specified deep generative models can converge faster and produce better results. The authors report state-of-the-art semi-supervised performance on MNIST, SVHN, and NORB. These outcomes support the value of improving the variational approximation and model specification, with the convergence claim presented as a finding suggested by the study.
icml-2016-auxiliary-deep-generative-mode.tldr: Auxiliary variables make variational inference more expressive, with reported gains in convergence and semi-supervised learning performance.

paragraphs: The paper introduces black-box alpha, an approximate inference method that minimizes a family of discrepancies called alpha divergences. The parameter alpha changes the criterion used to construct the approximation. This gives a single method a way to explore different inference behaviors instead of committing to one fixed divergence.

The procedure can use stochastic gradient descent, allowing it to scale to large datasets. Applying it requires the model’s likelihood function and its gradients, which can be obtained through automatic differentiation. As alpha approaches zero, the method approaches variational Bayes. At alpha equal to one, it yields an algorithm similar to expectation propagation, connecting two familiar approaches within one adjustable framework.

Experiments cover probit regression and neural-network regression and classification. In these experiments, intermediate or otherwise non-standard alpha settings, including one-half, usually yield better predictions than the variational-Bayes and expectation-propagation-like endpoints. The results suggest that choosing the divergence parameter can matter for predictive performance; they do not establish one alpha value as universally best.
icml-2016-black-box-alpha-divergence-min.tldr: Black-box alpha provides scalable approximate inference with a tunable divergence whose intermediate settings often improve predictions in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses black-box convex optimization in situations where computing gradients is expensive. A gradient provides information about how an objective changes, but obtaining that information can itself be a substantial part of the optimization cost. The authors propose a new framework designed with this setting in mind.

Within the framework, they derive a method that draws on several ideas from convex optimization. These include familiar first-order approaches such as gradient descent, quasi-Newton methods, and analytical centers. The abstract defines analytical centers through the minimization of self-concordant barriers. Bringing these concepts together is the methodological contribution: the proposed technique combines tools with different roles in organizing a convex optimization procedure.

The authors evaluate the resulting method empirically and report favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art algorithms, including BFGS. This supplies practical evidence for the framework in the setting studied. The stated scope is convex optimization with costly gradient computations, and the reported finding concerns empirical comparative performance within that scope.
icml-2016-black-box-optimization-with-a-.tldr: A framework combining convex optimization techniques compares favorably with established methods when gradient computations are expensive.

paragraphs: The paper develops algorithms for personalized course recommendations and curriculum design using logged student data. Personalization is challenging because students differ in their knowledge, learning behavior, and goals. The proposed approach uses historical observations to inform recommendations while explicitly addressing the reliability of the predictions used to make them.

The algorithms build on a regression estimator for contextual multi-armed bandits and add a variance penalty. This connects recommendation to a framework in which the usefulness of a choice depends on the student’s context. The variance term makes variability part of the recommendation criterion. The authors provide predictive-performance guarantees using empirical Bernstein bounds, giving the approach a statistical basis for assessing its predictions.

The paper also provides guidance for incorporating expert domain knowledge into recommendations. Its empirical illustration uses logged data from undergraduate engineering students at a post-secondary institution. Together, these contributions combine historical-data modeling, uncertainty-sensitive evaluation, and expert input in an approach to educational recommendations and curriculum design.
icml-2016-bounded-off-policy-evaluation-.tldr: Course recommendation algorithms combine logged student data, variance-penalized prediction, statistical guarantees, and guidance for incorporating expert knowledge.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes extend Gaussian processes into multilayer probabilistic models. They are formally equivalent to neural networks with multiple infinitely wide hidden layers. The paper motivates them as potentially offering greater flexibility, generalization capacity, and better-calibrated uncertainty than alternative deep models, while addressing the difficulty of learning them at useful scales.

The main contribution is an approximate Bayesian learning scheme that makes these models applicable to medium- and large-scale regression problems. It combines approximate expectation propagation with an efficient extension of probabilistic backpropagation. This learning procedure is the practical link between the expressive model family and nonlinear regression tasks involving real datasets.

Across eleven real-world datasets, the method outperforms Gaussian-process regression in every reported comparison and almost always exceeds the considered state-of-the-art approximate inference methods for Bayesian neural networks. Those comparisons include deterministic and sampling-based methods. The paper also analyzes six approximate Bayesian neural-network training methods, providing a broader empirical context for assessing the new deep Gaussian-process approach.
icml-2016-deep-gaussian-processes-for-re.tldr: An approximate Bayesian learning scheme makes deep Gaussian processes practical for larger regression tasks and performs strongly across eleven datasets.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian computation supports inference when a generative model’s likelihood is too expensive or intractable to evaluate. It compares simulated and observed data through summary statistics. Choosing those summaries is crucial: the information they preserve affects the likelihood approximation and, consequently, the quality of the resulting posterior sample.

DR-ABC learns the relationship between data and summary statistics that are optimal relative to a chosen loss function. It uses kernel-based distribution regression, treating distributions as inputs to this learning problem. The authors also extend the method to regression from conditional distributions, allowing the construction to account for the specific structure of the proposed generative model.

The framework uses random Fourier features for a computationally and statistically efficient implementation of large-scale kernel learning. In experiments on toy and real-world data, including hierarchical and time-series models, it substantially outperforms the related methods considered. The contribution is a principled route to constructing useful summaries, with optimality tied to the selected loss.
icml-2016-dr-abc-approximate-bayesian-co.tldr: DR-ABC learns loss-specific summary statistics through kernel distribution regression to improve approximate Bayesian computation.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling is commonly used to estimate marginal distributions through Markov chain Monte Carlo. Running updates asynchronously offers a way to parallelize the computation, and earlier empirical findings suggested that this could work efficiently for many models. However, the usual Markov-chain analysis does not directly apply to the asynchronous setting.

This paper develops a better theoretical understanding of two central issues: bias and mixing time. Bias concerns whether the sampling procedure systematically departs from the distribution it is intended to represent. Mixing time concerns how quickly the procedure reaches useful sampling behavior. Both matter when assessing whether a faster execution strategy also delivers reliable distribution estimates.

The authors compare their theoretical results with practical outcomes and report that experiments agree with the analysis. The contribution therefore connects the behavior of asynchronous Gibbs sampling to a more explicit theoretical account. It helps explain the reliability and speed questions raised by asynchronous execution, rather than judging the approach solely by how quickly updates can be performed.
icml-2016-ensuring-rapid-mixing-and-low-.tldr: The paper analyzes bias and mixing time in asynchronous Gibbs sampling and finds experimental agreement with its theoretical results.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a classifier’s true accuracy can be estimated using data without known labels. It also studies a closely related problem: when several classifiers perform the same task, how should their outputs be combined using estimates of their individual accuracies? Both questions make reliability estimation central to using classifier predictions.

The authors first introduce a simple graphical model that performs well in practice. They then develop two nonparametric extensions that improve its performance. The models provide a Bayesian approach to estimating accuracy from unlabeled observations, and those estimates also support combining multiple classifier outputs. This links evaluating the classifiers to using them together.

Experiments on two real-world datasets produce accuracy estimates within a few percent of the true values using only unlabeled data. The models also outperform the existing state-of-the-art solutions considered in both accuracy estimation and output combination. These findings demonstrate useful empirical accuracy in the tested settings, without making the reported error range a guarantee for every dataset.
icml-2016-estimating-accuracy-from-unlab.tldr: Bayesian graphical models estimate classifier accuracy from unlabeled data and improve the combination of multiple classifiers in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies macro F-measure maximization in extreme multi-label classification, where each example may receive multiple labels from an extremely large label space. The central difficulty is computational: a prediction strategy that works for a small number of labels can become expensive when the label space grows dramatically.

The authors build on results showing that F-measure can be maximized by appropriately thresholding conditional class-probability estimates. They examine several adaptations of this idea and show that a naive application is costly in the extreme-label setting. Their proposed solution uses classifiers that efficiently produce sparse probability estimates, restricting their output to the most probable labels.

This makes the availability of useful probability estimates part of the computational design of the classifier. The approach seeks to retain the benefits of probability-based thresholding while handling the scale of the label space. Empirical results provide evidence of strong practical performance, supporting sparse estimation as a useful strategy for pursuing F-measure in extreme multi-label problems.
icml-2016-extreme-f-measure-maximization.tldr: Sparse probability estimates make probability-thresholding approaches to F-measure practical for extremely large multi-label problems.

paragraphs: The paper proposes sparsemax, an activation function that produces probabilities with some entries exactly zero. This makes it possible for a model’s probability output to concentrate on a selected subset of alternatives. The idea is relevant both to predicting multiple labels and to attention mechanisms that allocate weight across pieces of information.

The authors derive sparsemax’s properties and show how to compute its Jacobian efficiently, enabling training through backpropagation. They also introduce a smooth, convex loss that plays a role analogous to logistic loss for softmax. A further theoretical result connects this loss to the Huber classification loss, relating the new training objective to an existing loss formulation.

Experiments show promising results on multi-label classification and attention-based natural language inference. In the latter setting, sparsemax achieves performance similar to traditional softmax while producing a more selective and compact attention focus. The result demonstrates that a sparser attention pattern can be obtained without sacrificing comparable task performance in the reported comparison.
icml-2016-from-softmax-to-sparsemax-a-sp.tldr: Sparsemax produces sparse probabilities and supports compact attention with performance similar to softmax in the reported inference experiments.

paragraphs: Tensor estimation models higher-order relationships among several data sources, with applications including multi-task learning, recommendation, and spatiotemporal analysis. This paper studies the statistical efficiency of a nonlinear version of that problem. It extends a common linear tensor-learning formulation into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and proposes a nonparametric Bayesian estimator based on Gaussian processes.

The central theoretical result establishes a statistical convergence rate without assuming strong convexity, including restricted strong convexity. The authors show that the rate is minimax optimal. In the problem setting analyzed, this means that the estimator matches the best achievable worst-case statistical rate, giving a precise efficiency claim for the proposed nonlinear method.

The authors also apply the estimator to multi-task learning and evaluate it on real-world datasets. They report substantial improvements over existing methods in those experiments. The paper thus combines a statistical optimality result for its formulation with empirical evidence that the nonlinear Gaussian-process approach can improve practical multi-task prediction.
icml-2016-gaussian-process-nonparametric.tldr: A Gaussian-process tensor estimator achieves a minimax-optimal convergence rate without strong-convexity assumptions and improves reported multi-task learning results.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a tree-based sampling procedure for estimating large weighted sums. Its goal is to prioritize computation while keeping the estimates unbiased. Inspired by Monte Carlo Tree Search, the method dynamically adjusts importance-based sampling so that computational effort can focus on samples with particularly large contributions.

The key step is to express a score, such as a loss or prediction estimate, as an empirical expectation. Samples occupy the tree’s leaves, and the tree helps direct attention toward troublesome heavy-weight samples. This formulation makes the procedure applicable both during learning on very large training sets and when evaluating models whose predictions involve many terms.

The authors illustrate the method with AdaBoost and a multilayer perceptron on large synthetic tasks, a convolutional network trained on millions of CIFAR deformations, and an SVM with hundreds of thousands of support vectors. Across these cases, they report computation reductions exceeding an order of magnitude, better loss estimates, or both, demonstrating several uses of the same estimation strategy.
icml-2016-importance-sampling-tree-for-l.tldr: An adaptive importance-sampling tree focuses computation on influential samples while preserving unbiased weighted-sum estimates.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear bandits when reward noise has heavy tails. Much prior work assumes bounded or sub-Gaussian noise, but the authors point out that these assumptions can fail in settings such as financial markets. The question is whether a learner can still control its cumulative decision-making loss under weaker noise conditions.

The authors propose two algorithms: one uses dynamic truncation, and the other uses a median-of-means estimator. Both are designed to handle noise through methods that are robust to unusually large observations. They derive regret bounds when the noise has only a finite moment of order one plus epsilon, making the relationship between tail behavior and learning performance explicit.

In particular, both algorithms guarantee sublinear regret when the noise has finite variance. This means regret per decision decreases over time under that sufficient condition. Experiments also show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art bounded-noise methods when the maximum noise bound is large but the relevant moment remains small, supporting the practical value of the weaker noise formulation.
icml-2016-no-regret-algorithms-for-heavy.tldr: Two robust linear-bandit algorithms handle heavy-tailed noise and guarantee sublinear regret when the noise has finite variance.

paragraphs: Noisy non-negative matrix factorization seeks two non-negative matrices whose product explains an observed matrix up to noise. Earlier polynomial-time guarantees required every noise column to be small relative to its signal column. The paper argues that this condition is restrictive for topic modeling and high-noise models, where almost every column may violate it.

The authors introduce a heavy-noise model requiring small average noise over large subsets of columns. Their algorithm, TSVDNMF, solves the problem under stated assumptions on the factors. Its assumption on the first factor is weaker than separability, while the paper supplies empirical justification for assumptions on the second. The error guarantees match previous algorithms, with a better stated running time.

The paper also proves uniqueness of the first factor without relying on separability or difficult-to-check geometric conditions. Its noise model covers cases of theoretical and practical interest. Empirical comparisons show improvements in both runtime and error over earlier polynomial-time algorithms, especially under high noise, supporting the usefulness of relaxing column-by-column noise restrictions.
icml-2016-non-negative-matrix-factorizat.tldr: TSVDNMF handles an aggregate heavy-noise condition with matching prior error guarantees and improved runtime under assumptions on the factors.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to generate a Poisson process governed by a hierarchical completely random measure without explicitly constructing the measure’s infinitely many atoms. These random measures define a prior for the process, but their infinite representation creates a computational challenge. The authors seek an exact way to work with the resulting process directly.

They derive the point process’s marginal distribution by integrating out the underlying completely random measure. Using properties specific to Poisson processes, they obtain an exact generation procedure for the hierarchical-prior setting. They also derive Gibbs sampling strategies for hierarchical models based on a Chinese restaurant franchise sampling scheme, providing an additional route for inference.

As an example, the paper introduces the sum of generalized gamma processes and applies it to topic modeling. By placing a prior on this model’s parameters, the approach can determine power-law behavior in topics and words in a Bayesian fashion. This links the collapsed representation to a concrete modeling application with learnable distributional behavior.
icml-2016-on-collapsed-representation-of.tldr: Marginalizing hierarchical completely random measures enables exact Poisson-process generation without explicitly constructing infinitely many atoms.

paragraphs: The paper studies one-shot generalization: encountering a new concept once and then generating plausible variations of it. Its motivation is the human ability to infer useful structure from a single example. The authors develop deep generative models that combine neural-network representations with Bayesian reasoning to pursue this ability in machine learning.

Their models generate sequentially and are built around feedback and attention. These characteristics support a class of generative models reported to be among the state of the art in density estimation and image generation. The approach connects the quality of the generative model to its ability to produce variations after limited exposure to new examples.

The demonstrations cover unconditional sampling, generating new examples of a given concept, and generating examples from a family of concepts. Across these tasks, the authors report compelling, diverse samples and demonstrate generalization after seeing new examples only once. The contribution is a class of general-purpose generative models with demonstrated one-shot capabilities across the reported tasks.
icml-2016-one-shot-generalization-in-dee.tldr: Sequential generative models using feedback and attention demonstrate diverse generation from newly encountered examples seen only once.

paragraphs: Many information-retrieval tasks evaluate a selected set of items through a multivariate loss. The quality of the decision therefore depends on the set-level outcome. This paper studies how to minimize expected loss when retrieving relevant items from a presented set, with expectation taken over the joint distribution of item sets.

The main result shows that, for most multivariate losses, an optimal prediction can be obtained by ordering items according to their conditional probability of a positive label and selecting the top k. A result of this kind had previously been known for F-measure. The characterization reduces the structure of the optimal decision to a probability ranking and a choice of how many items to retrieve.

Using this characterization, the authors develop an algorithm for estimating optimal predictions in practice. For many losses, its runtime is quadratic in the number of items in the set. They also present benchmark comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, connecting the theoretical decision rule to an implementable prediction procedure.
icml-2016-optimal-classification-with-mu.tldr: For most multivariate losses, optimal retrieval ranks items by conditional relevance probability and selects an appropriate top-k subset.

paragraphs: The paper develops parallel and distributed versions of Frank-Wolfe optimization. It studies shared-memory execution with mini-batches and distributed execution in which updates may arrive late. Both versions use asynchronous computation wherever possible, addressing how optimization can benefit from multiple workers without requiring every computation to proceed in lockstep.

The methods assume block-separable constraints, as in block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe. Their analysis includes that earlier method and identifies problem-dependent quantities that determine potential speedups. A notable property is that the guarantees depend only mildly on expected delays rather than requiring a worst-case bound on every delay. This supports robustness to stragglers and faulty worker threads.

Experiments on structural SVM and Group Fused Lasso problems show substantial speedups over the competing methods considered, including synchronous approaches. The contribution combines empirical acceleration with an analysis that reflects variability in worker timing. It also makes clear that the achievable speedup depends on the optimization problem’s structure, rather than promising a uniform gain from parallelism.
icml-2016-parallel-and-distributed-block.tldr: Asynchronous Frank-Wolfe methods achieve reported parallel speedups with guarantees that depend mildly on expected worker delays.

paragraphs: PESMO addresses optimization with several expensive objectives. Its target is the Pareto set, which represents solutions offering different tradeoffs among objectives. The method uses Bayesian uncertainty to decide where to evaluate next, choosing evaluations intended to reduce uncertainty about that set as much as possible.

The acquisition function decomposes into a sum of objective-specific terms. This allows objectives to be evaluated separately, potentially at different costs, and helps allocate additional evaluations to difficult objectives. The paper also reports that PESMO’s computational cost grows linearly with the number of objectives, compared with exponential growth for other methods considered.

On synthetic and real-world problems, PESMO produces better recommendations using fewer evaluations than the comparison methods. The results also show that evaluating objectives separately can improve performance, particularly when there are many objectives. The contribution therefore combines an information-based search criterion with a decomposition that supports more flexible use of an expensive evaluation budget.
icml-2016-predictive-entropy-search-for-.tldr: PESMO reduces uncertainty about the Pareto set while allowing separate objective evaluations and linear cost scaling in the number of objectives.

paragraphs: Rich Component Analysis addresses multiple datasets that describe overlapping aspects of the same phenomenon. The goal is to recover patterns belonging to one view or a subset of views. For example, molecular and physiological measurements may share some structure, while a researcher wants to isolate molecular patterns uncorrelated with physiology.

The framework models each view as driven by a different collection of latent components. Each component may itself be a complex, high-dimensional distribution. The authors introduce algorithms based on cumulant extraction that provably learn individual components without requiring the other components to be modeled. This makes selective recovery of structure the central operation of the method.

The paper combines RCA with stochastic gradient descent in a general model-learning procedure. Experiments show substantial accuracy improvements on synthetic and real datasets in supervised and unsupervised tasks. The framework also enables learning latent-variable models from samples altered by complex perturbations, extending its use to situations where samples from the unperturbed model are unavailable.
icml-2016-rich-component-analysis-2abe4c.tldr: Rich Component Analysis recovers latent components from overlapping data views without needing to model the other components.

paragraphs: Learning a sparse model can be viewed as identifying which features and samples are active, then optimizing over them. Safe screening helps by identifying some inactive features or samples that can be excluded. This paper brings feature screening and sample screening together, extending a line of work that had studied the two separately.

The proposed procedure alternates between screening features and screening samples. Its central insight is that the steps can reinforce each other: the outcome of feature screening can improve the next sample-screening step, and sample screening can improve subsequent feature screening. Information gained on one side of the problem therefore supports further reductions on the other.

The authors theoretically investigate this synergy and then demonstrate its practical advantages through extensive numerical experiments involving many features and samples. The contribution is a coordinated screening process whose two parts exchange useful information. It offers a way to reduce the remaining optimization problem while retaining the safe-screening basis for identifying inactive elements.
icml-2016-simultaneous-safe-screening-of.tldr: Alternating safe feature and sample screening lets each step strengthen the other and reduce sparse-learning problems more effectively.

paragraphs: When training data is abundant, repeatedly processing the full dataset can be prohibitively expensive. This paper studies learning procedures that begin with a smaller effective sample and increase its size during optimization. The focus is on iterative methods such as stochastic gradient descent, where the amount of data used can change as learning progresses.

The motivation comes from variance-reduced methods, whose linear convergence rates scale favorably with smaller sample sizes. The proposed algorithm exploits that property through adaptive sample growth. Early optimization can benefit from working with fewer samples, while later stages incorporate more data to reach the accuracy supported by the full sample.

The authors establish speedups both theoretically and empirically. Their algorithm reaches statistical accuracy on an n-sample in 2n steps, compared with n log n steps. The target is statistical accuracy, tying the optimization effort to the accuracy available from the data. The result shows how controlling sample size can reduce the computational work needed to reach that target.
icml-2016-starting-small-learning-with-a.tldr: Adaptive sample growth exploits faster optimization on small samples to reach statistical accuracy in 2n rather than n log n steps.
